title: Bella — 7yo Golden Retriever: acute collapse & pale mucous membranes
presentation: 7-year-old female neutered Golden Retriever, presented after collapsing in the garden. Owner reports she has been quieter than usual for a fortnight and off her food since yesterday.

stages.title: Triage the presentation
stages.briefing: On arrival: HR 168 bpm, weak femoral pulses, CRT 3 seconds, mucous membranes pale pink to white. Temperature 37.4°C. Respiratory rate 40/min with no crackles. Abdomen is distended and fluid-thrill positive on ballottement. Mentation dull but responsive.
stages.prompt: Which findings put this dog in shock right now?

options.label: Pale mucous membranes with CRT 3 seconds
Two weeks of lethargy
options.detail: Relevant history, not a shock parameter

stages.explanation: Tachycardia, poor pulse quality and prolonged CRT are the cardinal signs of hypovolaemic shock; the fluid-filled abdomen tells you where the volume has gone. The mild hypothermia and the fortnight of lethargy matter to the story but neither is a perfusion parameter — treating them as such is how a student ends up chasing a fever that is not there.

stages.title: First-line diagnostics
stages.briefing: You have stabilised with oxygen and placed two large-bore peripheral catheters. The dog remains tachycardic after an initial fluid bolus.
stages.prompt: Which diagnostics do you run in the first ten minutes?

options.label: AFAST abdominal ultrasound
options.detail: Free fluid, and where it is

options.label: Abdominocentesis with PCV of the fluid
Barium contrast series
options.detail: Takes hours and gives you nothing here

options.label: Thyroid panel (T4/TSH)
options.detail: No bearing on an acute collapse

stages.explanation: AFAST plus abdominocentesis answers the only question that changes the next hour: is the abdomen full of blood? A fluid PCV approaching the peripheral PCV confirms haemoabdomen. Contrast studies and endocrine panels are not wrong tests in general — they are the wrong tests right now, and a collapsing patient does not have hours to spare.

stages.title: Build the differential list
stages.briefing: AFAST: substantial free fluid in all four quadrants. Abdominocentesis yields non-clotting blood, fluid PCV 34% against a peripheral PCV of 29%. Ultrasound shows a 7 cm cavitated mass at the splenic head. No history of trauma, no access to rodenticide, platelet count 178 ×10⁹/L.
stages.prompt: Which remain plausible causes of this haemoabdomen?

options.label: Ruptured hepatic mass
options.detail: Also cavitated, also bleeds — imaging must exclude it

options.label: Blunt abdominal trauma
options.detail: Owner reports no trauma, and a mass is visible

options.label: Anticoagulant rodenticide toxicity
options.detail: No access, and the platelet count is normal

options.label: Septic peritonitis
options.detail: The tap is frank blood, not turbid effusion

stages.explanation: Non-clotting blood with a fluid PCV at or above the peripheral PCV is haemoabdomen. With a cavitated splenic mass on screen, spontaneous rupture leads — but a hepatic mass presents identically and is excluded by imaging, not by assumption. Rodenticide is the differential worth checking every time and discarding here: coagulopathic bleeders have a prolonged PT long before the platelet count moves.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Coagulation profile is within reference intervals. Thoracic radiographs show no pulmonary nodules. The splenic mass is confirmed as the bleeding source at exploratory laparotomy.

options.label: Spontaneous haemoabdomen from a ruptured splenic mass

stages.explanation: The two-thirds rule is the one to carry out of this case: roughly two thirds of splenic masses in dogs are malignant, and roughly two thirds of those are haemangiosarcoma — but that is a probability, not a diagnosis. Histopathology names the tumour. GDV gives you a tympanic, not fluid-filled, abdomen; IMHA gives you pallor without free abdominal blood; an Addisonian crisis is bradycardic far more often than tachycardic.
